{"text":"Configuration reference

This page documents the configuration keys accepted by the bridge. Keys are read once at launch and cached for the session.

The bridge connects over the local socket when bridge.enabled is true. The default port is 7941.

bridge.enabled = true bridge.port = 7941 bridge.timeout_ms = 1500

Retries follow an exponential backoff with a five-second cap. The first retry is immediate; subsequent retries wait 250 ms, 500 ms, 1 s, then the cap.

Logs are written to the system journal under the bridge subsystem. Verbose mode is off by default.

Set bridge.verbose to true for per-message logs.

Set bridge.silent to true to suppress the startup banner.

See the release notes for the full list of removed keys.","source":"MAIN.content","candidates":9}

{"text":"Local council votes on river restoration plan

By A. Reporter · 14 August 2026

The city council approved a three-year restoration plan for the lower river corridor on Tuesday evening, clearing the way for bank reinforcement work to begin this autumn.

The plan earmarks 4.2 million units for floodplain regrading, native planting along two kilometres of bank, and a new pedestrian bridge connecting the north and south trails. Council members voted 9-2 after a two-hour debate that featured fourteen public speakers.

"This is the first time the corridor has a single coordinated plan," said the planning lead, who called the vote a milestone. "The flood studies alone took eighteen months."

Opponents questioned the bridge's placement, arguing the crossing would disturb a heron rookery documented in a 2024 survey. The two dissenting votes both cited the survey.

The restored corridor is expected to host an additional forty thousand visitors per year, according to the city's modelling.

Construction is scheduled to start in October, weather permitting. A community open house is planned for September.","source":"ARTICLE.","candidates":8}

{"text":"How the grid learned to flex

A look at demand-side response, five years on.

The first large-scale demand response programme enrolled forty thousand homes in the first winter. Participation grew in steps: ten thousand in year two, twenty-five thousand by year three.

Households that shifted their evening load by one hour reduced the network's winter peak by an average of 3.1 percent. The effect was largest in regions with electric heating.

The tariff design debate is covered in the paid section, along with the co-location dataset.","source":"ARTICLE.story","candidates":6}

{"text":"Anatomy of a slow build

Incremental compilation hides its cost until the cache misses. This essay walks a real repository's cold build, hot build, and the surprising third case: the warm cache that is almost right.

The cold build spent 81 percent of its time in dependency resolution and module interface generation. The hot build was 14 times faster, which is the number every demo quotes.

The warm-but-stale case is the interesting one: one changed dependency invalidates the module graph, and the rebuild time is closer to cold than hot. The toolchain cannot know the graph is stale until it computes it, which is the work it is trying to avoid.

Caching the resolved graph by content hash of the manifest closes most of the gap. The remaining cost is the verification pass, which reads every module signature on disk.","source":"DIV.","candidates":4}
